shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText: The greater part of mankind, my Paulinus, complains of the unkindness of Nature, because we are born only for a short space of time, and that this allotted period of life runs away so swiftly, nay so hurriedly, that with but few exceptions men's life comes to an end just as they are preparing to enjoy it: nor is it only the common herd and the ignorant vulgar who mourn over this universal misfortune, as they consider it to be: this reflection has wrung complaints even from great men. Hence comes that well-known saying of physicians, that art is long but life is short: hence arose that quarrel, so unbefitting a sage, which Aristotle picked with Nature, because she had indulged animals with such length of days that some of them lived for ten or fifteen centuries, while man, although born for many and such great exploits, had the term of his existence cut so much shorter.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: Most people, Paulinus, complain that nature has been unfair to us. They say we are born with too little time, and that even the time we are given slips away far too quickly — so fast that most people die just as they're getting ready to really live. It's not just ordinary people and the uneducated masses who grieve over what they see as this universal tragedy. Even great thinkers have complained about it. That's where doctors get their famous saying: 'Art is long, but life is short.' That's also why Aristotle — a wise man who should have known better — picked a fight with Nature herself. He was angry that she gave some animals lifespans of ten or fifteen centuries, while humans, despite being capable of such great things, got such a brief time on earth.

shortness-of-life_section-01.originalText: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry out the most important projects: we have an ample portion, if we do but arrange the whole of it aright: but when it all runs to waste through luxury and carelessness, when it is not devoted to any good purpose, then at the last we are forced to feel that it is all over, although we never noticed how it glided away. Thus it is: we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them. When great and kinglike riches fall into the hands of a bad master, they are dispersed straightway, but even a moderate fortune, when bestowed upon a wise guardian, increases by use: and in like manner our life has great opportunities for one who knows how to dispose of it to the best advantage.
shortness-of-life_section-01.plainEnglish: We haven't been given a short life. We've just wasted a lot of it. Life is long enough to do great things — if you stop throwing it away. We have plenty of time, but only if we use it right. When we waste our days on luxury and laziness, when we don't spend them on anything worthwhile, we suddenly realize it's all over. We never even noticed how quickly it slipped by. Here's the truth: we don't get a short life. We make it short. We're not poor in days — we're wasteful with them. When great wealth falls into the hands of a bad owner, it disappears right away. But even a modest fortune grows when it's given to a wise manager. Our life works the same way. It offers great opportunities to anyone who knows how to use it well.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Why do we complain about Nature? She has been kind to us. Life is long enough — if you know how to use it.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: One man is possessed by an avarice which nothing can satisfy, another by a laborious diligence in doing what is totally useless: another is sodden by wine: another is benumbed by sloth: one man is exhausted by an ambition which makes him court the good will of others: another, through his eagerness as a merchant, is led to visit every land and every sea by the hope of gain: some are plagued by the love of soldiering, and are always either endangering other men's lives or in trembling for their own: some wear away their lives in that voluntary slavery, the
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: One man is driven by greed that can never be satisfied. Another wastes his energy on completely pointless tasks. Another drowns himself in wine. Another is paralyzed by laziness. One man exhausts himself chasing ambition, desperately trying to win people's approval. Another becomes a merchant and travels to every corner of the world, hoping to get rich. Some are obsessed with warfare — they're always either putting others in danger or fearing for their own lives. Others waste their lives in voluntary slavery, the

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: unrequited service of great men: many are occupied either in laying claim to other men's fortune or in complaining of their own: a great number have no settled purpose, and are tossed from one new scheme to another by a rambling, inconsistent, dissatisfied, fickle habit of mind: some care for no object sufficiently to try to attain it, but lie lazily yawning until their fate comes upon them: so that I cannot doubt the truth of that verse which the greatest of poets has dressed in the guise of an oracular response— "We live a small part only of our lives."
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: They chase after powerful people who will never return their loyalty. Many spend their time either trying to grab other people's money or whining about their own situation. A huge number have no clear goals at all. They drift from one half-baked plan to another, restless and never satisfied with anything. Some people don't care enough about any goal to actually pursue it. They just lie around lazily until fate catches up with them. So I have no doubt that the greatest poet was right when he wrote those words like a prophecy: 'We live only a small part of our lives.'

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: But all duration is time, not life: vices press upon us and surround us on every side, and do not permit us to regain our feet, or to raise our eyes and gaze upon truth, but when we are down keep us prostrate and chained to low desires. Men who are in this condition are never allowed to come to themselves: if ever by chance they obtain any rest, they roll to and fro like the deep sea, which heaves and tosses after a gale, and they never have any respite from their lusts.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: But all duration is time, not life. Vices press in on us from every side. They don't let us get back on our feet or lift our heads to see the truth. When we're down, they keep us flat on the ground, chained to shallow desires. People trapped like this never get a chance to find themselves. Even when they get a brief break, they roll back and forth like the ocean that keeps heaving and tossing after a storm. They never get any rest from their cravings.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Do you suppose that I speak of those whose ills are notorious? Nay, look at those whose prosperity all men run to see: they are choked by their own good things. To how many men do riches prove a heavy burden? how many men's eloquence and continual desire to display their own cleverness has cost them their lives? how many are sallow with constant sensual indulgence? how many have no freedom left them by the tribe of clients that surges around them? Look through all these, from the lowest to the highest:—this man calls his friends to support him, this one is present in court, this one is the defendant, this one pleads for him, this one is on the jury: but no one lays claim to his own self, every one wastes his time over some one else.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: You think I'm only talking about people with obvious problems? No, look at those everyone envies — the successful ones. They're drowning in their own good fortune. How many rich people are crushed by their wealth? How many speakers have died because they couldn't stop showing off how clever they were? How many have made themselves sick with constant pleasure-seeking? How many have lost all freedom because they're surrounded by crowds of people wanting favors? Look at everyone, from bottom to top. This man calls friends to help him. That one appears in court. Another defends himself. Someone else argues his case. Another sits on the jury. But nobody claims time for himself. Everyone wastes their life on someone else.

shortness-of-life_section-02.originalText: Investigate those men, whose names are in every one's mouth: you will find that they bear just the same marks: A is devoted to B, and B to C: no one belongs to himself. Moreover some men are full of most irrational anger: they complain of the insolence of their chiefs, because they have not granted them an audience when they wished for it; as if a man had any right to complain of being so haughtily shut out by another, when he never has leisure to give his own conscience a hearing. This chief of yours, whoever he is, though he may look at you in an offensive manner, still will some day look at you, open his ears to your words, and give you a seat by his side: but you never design to look upon yourself, to listen to your own grievances. You ought not, then, to claim these services from another, especially since while you yourself were doing so, you did not wish for an interview with another man, but were not able to obtain one with yourself.
shortness-of-life_section-02.plainEnglish: Look closely at those famous people everyone talks about. You'll see they all have the same problem: Person A serves Person B, and Person B serves Person C. No one belongs to himself. Some people get irrationally angry about this. They complain that their bosses are arrogant for not granting them a meeting when they wanted one. But how can you complain about someone else shutting you out when you never give yourself time to listen to your own conscience? That boss of yours might look at you rudely now, but someday he will look at you, listen to your words, and give you a seat next to him. But you never bother to look at yourself or listen to your own complaints. You shouldn't expect these services from others, especially since when you were chasing after them, you didn't want a meeting with someone else — you just couldn't get one with yourself.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Were all the brightest intellects of all time to employ themselves on this one subject, they never could sufficiently express their wonder at this blindness of men's minds: men will not allow any one to establish himself upon their estates, and upon the most trifling dispute about the measuring of boundaries, they betake themselves to stones and cudgels: yet they allow others to encroach upon their lives, nay, they themselves actually lead others in to take possession of them. You cannot find any one who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does every one distribute his life? men covetously guard their property from waste, but when it comes to waste of time, they are most prodigal of that of which it would become them to be sparing.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Even if all the greatest minds in history worked together on this problem, they could never fully express how amazed they are by human blindness. People won't let anyone set foot on their property. They'll grab stones and clubs over the tiniest boundary dispute. Yet they let others take over their lives. In fact, they actually invite people in to waste their time. You can't find anyone who wants to give away their money. But everyone gives away their life to countless people. We jealously guard our possessions from being wasted. But when it comes to wasting time — the one thing we should protect most carefully — we throw it around like it's worthless.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Let us take one of the elders, and say to him, "We perceive that you have arrived at the extreme limits of human life: you are in your hundredth year, or even older. Come now, reckon up your whole life in black and white: tell us how much of your time has been spent upon your creditors, how much on your mistress, how much on your king, how much on your clients, how much in quarrelling with your wife, how much in keeping your slaves in order, how much in running up and down the city on business. Add to this the diseases which we bring upon us with our own hands, and the time which has laid idle without any use having been made of it; you will see that you have not lived as many years as you count.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Let's imagine talking to an old man and saying: "We see you've reached the very end of human life. You're a hundred years old, maybe more. Now sit down and add up your whole life honestly. Tell us how much time you spent dealing with people you owed money to. How much on your lover. How much serving your king. How much managing your clients. How much fighting with your wife. How much disciplining your slaves. How much running around the city on errands. Add in the diseases you brought on yourself, and all the time you just wasted doing nothing useful. You'll realize you haven't actually lived as many years as you think you have."

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: Look back in your memory and see how often you have been consistent in your projects, how many days passed as you intended them to do when you were at your own disposal, how often you did not change colour and your spirit did not quail, how much work you have done in so long a time, how many people have without your knowledge stolen parts of your life from you, how much you have lost, how large a part has been taken up by useless grief, foolish gladness, greedy desire, or polite conversation; how little of yourself is left to you: you will then perceive that you will die prematurely."
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: Look back and be honest with yourself. How often have you stuck to your plans? How many days went exactly as you wanted when you had complete control? How often did you stay calm and confident without losing your nerve? What have you actually accomplished in all this time? How many people have stolen pieces of your life without you even noticing? How much time have you lost? How much has been eaten up by pointless worry, empty pleasures, endless wanting, or small talk? How little of yourself do you have left? When you see this clearly, you'll realize you're dying too young — not because life is short, but because you've given most of it away.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: What, then, is the reason of this? It is that people live as though they would live for ever: you never remember your human frailty; you never notice how much of your time has already gone by: you spend it as though you had an abundant and overflowing store of it, though all the while that day which you devote to some man or to some thing is perhaps your last. You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: What's the reason for this? People live as if they'll never die. You forget how fragile you are. You don't notice how much time has already slipped away. You spend it as if you had endless amounts, even though the day you're wasting on someone or something might be your last. You fear everything like the mortal you are, but you want everything as if you'll live forever.

shortness-of-life_section-03.originalText: You will hear many men say, "After my fiftieth year I will give myself up to leisure: my sixtieth shall be my last year of public office": and what guarantee have you that your life will last any longer? who will let all this go on just as you have arranged it? are you not ashamed to reserve only the leavings of your life for yourself, and appoint for the enjoyment of your own right mind only that time which you cannot devote to any business? How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it! What a foolish forgetfulness of our mortality, to put off wholesome counsels until our fiftieth or sixtieth year, and to choose that our lives shall begin at a point which few of us ever reach.
shortness-of-life_section-03.plainEnglish: You'll hear many people say, "After I turn fifty, I'll finally have time for myself. When I'm sixty, I'll retire from public life." But what makes you think you'll live that long? Who says everything will work out exactly as you planned? Aren't you embarrassed to save only the scraps of your life for yourself? You're planning to enjoy your own mind only during the years when you can't do any real work anymore. How foolish to start living just when you have to die! What a stupid way to forget that we're mortal — putting off wise decisions until you're fifty or sixty, deciding that your real life will begin at an age most people never even reach.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy. Sometimes they would fain descend from their lofty pedestal, if it could be safely done: for Fortune collapses by its own weight, without any shock or interference from without.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: You'll notice that the most powerful and important people often say they wish they had more free time. They praise it and say they'd rather have leisure than all the privileges they currently enjoy. Sometimes they want to step down from their high positions — if only they could do it safely. But power often destroys itself under its own weight, even without any outside attack.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: The late Emperor Augustus, upon whom the gods bestowed more blessings than on any one else, never ceased to pray for rest and exemption from the troubles of empire: he used to enliven his labours with this sweet, though unreal consolation, that he would some day live for himself alone. In a letter which he addressed to the Senate, after promising that his rest shall not be devoid of dignity nor discreditable to his former glories, I find the following words:—"These things, however, it is more honourable to do than to promise: but my eagerness for that time, so earnestly longed for, has led me to derive a certain pleasure from speaking about it, though the reality is still far distant." He thought leisure so important, that though he could not actually enjoy it, yet he did so by anticipation and by thinking about it.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: Even Emperor Augustus — who received more gifts from the gods than anyone else — never stopped hoping for rest and a break from running the empire. He would comfort himself during his long work days with a sweet but impossible dream: that someday he would live only for himself. In a letter to the Senate, he promised that his retirement would still be dignified and wouldn't dishonor his past achievements. Then he wrote: "It's better to actually do these things than just promise them. But I'm so eager for that time I long for that I get pleasure just from talking about it, even though it's still far away." He valued free time so much that even though he couldn't have it, he enjoyed it by imagining it and thinking about it.

shortness-of-life_section-04.originalText: While he was pacifying the Alpine regions, and subduing the enemies whom he found in the midst of the Roman empire, while he was extending its boundaries beyond the Rhine, the Euphrates, and the Danube, at Rome itself the swords of Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were being sharpened to slay him. Scarcely had he escaped from their plot, when his already failing age was terrified by his daughter and all the noble youths who were pledged to her cause by adultery with her by way of oath of fidelity. Then there was Paulus and Antonius's mistress, a second time to be feared by Rome: and when he had cut out these ulcers from his very limbs, others grew in their place: the empire, like a body overloaded with blood, was always breaking out somewhere. For this reason he longed for leisure: all his labours were based upon hopes and thoughts of leisure: this was the wish of him who could accomplish the wishes of all other men.
shortness-of-life_section-04.plainEnglish: While Augustus was conquering the Alpine regions and defeating enemies within the Roman empire itself, while he was pushing the borders beyond the Rhine, Euphrates, and Danube rivers, back in Rome conspirators like Murena, Caepio, Lepidus, Egnatius, and others were sharpening their swords to kill him. He barely escaped their plot when his failing health was shaken by his own daughter's scandal — she had slept with young nobles who swore loyalty to her through adultery. Then came the threat of Paulus and Mark Antony's mistress, dangerous to Rome once again. When he cut out these infected parts of his body, new ones grew back. The empire was like a body with too much blood — always bursting somewhere. That's why he craved peace and quiet. All his hard work was driven by the hope of someday having leisure. The man who could grant everyone else's wishes had this one wish for himself.

shortness-of-life_section-05.originalText:
While tossed hither and thither by Catiline and Clodius, Pompeius
and Crassus, by some open enemies and some doubtful friends, while
he struggled with the struggling republic and kept it from going
to ruin, when at last he was banished, being neither able to keep
silence in prosperity nor to endure adversity with patience, how
often must Marcus Cicero have cursed that consulship of his which
he never ceased to praise, and which nevertheless deserved it? What
piteous expressions he uses in a letter to Atticus when Pompeius
the father had been defeated, and his son was recruiting his shattered
forces in Spain?
shortness-of-life_section-05.plainEnglish: Think about Marcus Cicero. He was thrown around by Catiline and Clodius, by Pompey and Crassus — some open enemies, some questionable friends. He fought to save the struggling republic from collapse. When he was finally banished, he couldn't stay quiet when things went well or handle trouble with grace. How often must he have cursed that consulship he never stopped bragging about (even though he deserved the praise)? You can see his despair in a letter to Atticus, written after Pompey the elder was defeated and his son was trying to rebuild his broken army in Spain.

shortness-of-life_section-05.originalText:
“Do you ask,” writes he, “what I am doing here? I
am living in my Tusculan villa almost as a prisoner.” He adds more
afterwards, wherein he laments his former life, complains of the
present, and despairs of the future. Cicero called himself “half a
prisoner,” but, by Hercules, the wise man never would have come
under so lowly a title: he never would be half a prisoner, but would
always enjoy complete and entire liberty, being free, in his own
power, and greater than all others: for what can be greater than
the man who is greater than Fortune?
shortness-of-life_section-05.plainEnglish: "Do you ask," Cicero writes, "what I'm doing here? I'm living at my villa near Rome almost like a prisoner." Then he goes on to complain about his past life, grumble about the present, and lose hope about the future. Cicero called himself "half a prisoner." But by God, a wise man would never accept such a pathetic label. He would never be half a prisoner. He would always enjoy complete freedom — free, in control of himself, and greater than everyone else. What could be greater than someone who has conquered Fortune itself?

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: When Livius Drusus, a vigorous and energetic man, brought forward bills for new laws and radical measures of the Gracchus pattern, being the centre of a vast mob of all the peoples of Italy, and seeing no way to solve the question, since he was not allowed to deal with it as he wished, and yet was not free to throw it up after having once taken part in it, complained bitterly of his life, which had been one of unrest from the very cradle, and said, we are told, that "he was the only person who had never had any holidays even when he was a boy." Indeed, while he was still under age and wearing the praetexta, he had the courage to plead the cause of accused persons in court, and to make use of his influence so powerfully that it is well known that in some causes his exertions gained a verdict.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: Take Livius Drusus — a strong, energetic man who proposed new laws and radical reforms like the Gracchi brothers had done. He found himself surrounded by huge crowds from all over Italy. But he couldn't see any way forward. He wasn't allowed to handle things the way he wanted, yet he couldn't just walk away after getting involved. So he complained bitterly about his life, saying it had been restless from the day he was born. He supposedly said, "I'm the only person who never had any holidays, not even as a child." And it's true — even when he was still a minor wearing the toga praetexta, he had the nerve to defend accused people in court. He used his influence so powerfully that everyone knew he won several cases through sheer effort.

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: Where would such precocious ambition stop? You may be sure that one who showed such boldness as a child would end by becoming a great pest both in public and in private life: it was too late for him to complain that he had had no holidays, when from his boyhood he had been a firebrand and a nuisance in the courts.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: Where would such early ambition lead? You can be sure that a child who showed such boldness would grow up to be a real problem in both public and private life. It would be too late for him to complain that he never had any time off, when from boyhood he had been a troublemaker and a pest in the courts.

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: It is a stock question whether he committed suicide: for he fell by a sudden wound in the groin, and some doubted whether his death was caused by his own hand, though none disputed its having happened most seasonably. It would be superfluous to mention more who, while others thought them the happiest of men, have themselves borne true witness to their own feelings, and have loathed all that they have done for all the years of their lives: yet by these complaints they have effected no alteration either in others or in themselves: for after these words have escaped them their feelings revert to their accustomed frame.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: People still debate whether he killed himself. He died from a sudden wound to his groin, and some wondered if he did it to himself. But no one questioned that his death came at just the right time. I could mention many more examples like this. These are men that others thought were the happiest people alive. Yet they told the truth about how they really felt. They hated everything they had spent years doing with their lives. But their complaints changed nothing — not in other people, and not even in themselves. After speaking these words, their feelings just went back to the same old patterns.

shortness-of-life_section-06.originalText: By Hercules, that life of you great men, even though it should last for more than a thousand years, is still a very short one: those vices of yours would swallow up any extent of time: no wonder if this our ordinary span, which, though Nature hurries on, can be enlarged by common sense, soon slips away from you; for you do not lay hold of it or hold it back, and try to delay the swiftest of all things, but you let it pass as though it were a useless thing and you could supply its place.
shortness-of-life_section-06.plainEnglish: By God, even if you powerful men lived for a thousand years, your lives would still be short. Your vices would devour any amount of time you were given. No wonder our normal lifespan — which nature rushes along but wisdom can stretch — slips through your fingers so quickly. You don't grab hold of time or try to slow it down. You let the fastest thing in the world just pass by, as if it were worthless and you could always get more.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Among these I reckon in the first place those who devote their time to nothing but drinking and debauchery: for no men are busied more shamefully: the others, although the glory which they pursue is but a counterfeit, still deserve some credit for their pursuit of it—though you may tell me of misers, of passionate men, of men who hate and who even wage war without a cause—yet all such men sin like men: but the sin of those who are given up to gluttony and lust is a disgraceful one. Examine all the hours of their lives: consider how much time they spend in calculation, how much in plotting, how much in fear, how much in giving and deceiving flattery, how much in entering into recognizances for themselves or for others, how much in banquets, which indeed become a serious business, you will see that they are not allowed any breathing time either by their pleasures or their pains.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Among the time-wasters, I put drunks and party animals at the top of the list. No one wastes time more shamefully than they do. At least other people — even if they chase fake glory — deserve some credit for trying. You can name all the misers, the angry people, the ones who hate and fight for no reason. Sure, they're all sinning. But at least they sin like human beings. The sin of gluttons and perverts is just disgusting. Look at how these people spend their hours. Count up the time they spend scheming, plotting, being afraid, giving fake compliments, making promises for themselves and others, throwing banquets that become serious business ventures. You'll see that their pleasures and pains give them no rest at all.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Finally, all are agreed that nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it. No man knows less about living than a business man: there is nothing about which it is more difficult to gain knowledge. Other arts have many folk everywhere who profess to teach them: some of them can be so thoroughly learned by mere boys, that they are able to teach them to others: but one's whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one's whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Everyone agrees on this: you can't do anything well — whether it's speaking or writing — if your mind is busy with something else. Nothing takes root in a mind that's pulled in different directions and pushes away whatever you try to put into it. No one knows less about living than someone obsessed with business. There's nothing harder to learn than how to live. Other skills have plenty of teachers everywhere. Some can be learned so well by children that they can teach them to others. But learning how to live takes your entire lifetime. And here's what might surprise you even more: learning how to die takes your entire lifetime too.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Many excellent men have freed themselves from all hindrances, have given up riches, business, and pleasure, and have made it their duty to the very end of their lives to learn how to live: and yet the larger portion of them leave this life confessing that they do not yet know how to live, and still less know how to live as wise men. Believe me, it requires a great man and one who is superior to human frailties not to allow any of his time to be filched from him: and therefore it follows that his life is a very long one, because he devotes every possible part of it to himself: no portion lies idle or uncultivated, or in another man's power; for he finds nothing worthy of being exchanged for his time, which he husbands most grudgingly.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Many great people have given up everything that held them back. They abandoned wealth, work, and pleasure to spend their whole lives learning how to live well. Yet most of them die admitting they still don't know how to live — let alone how to live wisely. Trust me, it takes an extraordinary person to protect their time from being stolen. Someone who rises above ordinary human weaknesses. That's why such a person's life feels very long. They dedicate every moment to themselves. No time sits wasted or neglected or under someone else's control. They find nothing valuable enough to trade for their time, which they guard fiercely.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Balance your account, and run over all the days of your life; you will see that only a very few days, and only those which were useless for any other purpose, have been left to you.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Take stock of your life and look back at all your days. You'll see that only a few days — and only the ones that were useless for anything else — were truly yours.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: He who has obtained the _fasces_[6] for which he longed, is eager to get rid of them, and is constantly saying, "When will this year be over?" another exhibits public games, and once would have given a great deal for the chance of doing so, but now "when," says he, "shall I escape from this?" another is an advocate who is fought for in all the courts, and who draws immense audiences, who crowd all the forum to a far greater distance than they can hear him; "When," says he, "will vacation-time come?" Every man hurries through his life, and suffers from a yearning for the future, and a weariness of the present: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow: for what new pleasure can any hour now bestow upon him? he knows it all, and has indulged in it all even to satiety.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: The politician who finally gets the power he craved now wants to get rid of it. He keeps asking, "When will this term be over?" Another man puts on expensive public games — something he once would have paid anything to do. Now he asks, "When can I escape from this?" There's the famous lawyer who packs the courthouse, drawing crowds that stretch beyond where they can even hear him speak. He asks, "When does vacation start?" Everyone rushes through life. They long for the future and grow tired of the present. But the person who uses all his time for his own purposes — who plans each day like he's planning his whole life — doesn't wish for tomorrow or fear it. What new pleasure could any hour bring him? He's experienced everything already, even to the point of being sick of it.

shortness-of-life_section-07.originalText: Fortune may deal with the rest as she will, his life is already safe from her: such a man may gain something, but cannot lose anything: and, indeed, he can only gain anything in the same way as one who is already glutted and filled can get some extra food which he takes although he does not want it. You have no grounds, therefore, for supposing that any one has lived long, because he has wrinkles or grey hairs: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive. Why! would you think that a man had voyaged much if a fierce gale had caught him as soon as he left his port, and he had been driven round and round the same place continually by a succession of winds blowing from opposite quarters? such a man has not travelled much, he has only been much tossed about.
shortness-of-life_section-07.plainEnglish: Fortune can do whatever she wants with everything else — this man's life is already safe from her. He might gain something, but he can't lose anything. He can only gain things the way someone who's already stuffed full might get some extra food that he takes even though he doesn't want it. So don't think someone has lived long just because he has wrinkles or gray hair. That man hasn't lived long — he's just been alive for a long time. Would you say a sailor had traveled far if a storm caught him right after leaving port and kept spinning him around in circles with winds blowing from every direction? That man hasn't sailed much. He's just been tossed around a lot.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: I am filled with wonder when I see some men asking others for their time, and those who are asked for it most willing to give it: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself, as though in asking for this one asked for nothing, and in giving it one gave nothing: we play with what is the most precious of all things: yet it escapes men's notice, because it is an incorporeal thing, and because it does not come before our eyes; and therefore it is held very cheap, nay, hardly any value whatever is put upon it. Men set the greatest store upon presents or pensions, and hire out their work, their services, or their care in order to gain them: no one values time: they give it much more freely, as though it cost nothing.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: I'm amazed when I see people asking others for their time, and how willingly people give it away. Both sides think about what the time is for, but neither thinks about the time itself. It's as if asking for time means asking for nothing, and giving it away means giving nothing. We treat the most precious thing we have like a game. People don't notice this because time isn't something you can touch or see. So we think it's worthless — or nearly worthless. People treasure gifts and money. They work hard for pay, services, or favors. But no one values time. We give it away freely, as if it costs us nothing.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you will see these same people clasping the knees of their physician as suppliants when they are sick and in present peril of death, and if threatened with a capital charge willing to give all that they possess in order that they may live: so inconsistent are they. Indeed, if the number of every man's future years could be laid before him, as we can lay that of his past years, how anxious those who found that they had but few years remaining would be to make the most of them? Yet it is easy to arrange the distribution of a quantity, however small, if we know how much there is: what you ought to husband most carefully is that which may run short you know not when.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Yet these same people will beg their doctor on their knees when they're sick and facing death. If they're charged with a crime that could kill them, they'll give away everything they own just to stay alive. They're completely inconsistent. Imagine if everyone could see exactly how many years they have left, the way we can count the years behind us. Those who discovered they had only a few years remaining would be desperate to use them well. It's easy to manage any amount — even a small one — when you know exactly how much you have. But the thing you should guard most carefully is the one that could run out at any moment, and you don't know when.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: Yet you have no reason to suppose that they do not know how dear a thing time is: they are wont to say to those whom they especially love that they are ready to give them a part of their own years. They do give them, and know not that they are giving them; but they give them in such a manner that they themselves lose them without the others gaining them. They do not, however, know whence they obtain their supply, and therefore they are able to endure the waste of what is not seen: yet no one will give you back your years, no one will restore them to you again: your life will run its course when once it has begun, and will neither begin again or efface what it has done.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: But don't think these people don't understand how precious time is. They often tell the people they love most that they would gladly give them some of their own years. And they do give them — without even realizing it. But they give in a way where they lose the time while the other person doesn't actually gain it. They don't understand where their time comes from, so they can stand to waste what they can't see. But no one will give your years back to you. No one will restore them. Once your life starts moving, it won't start over or undo what's already been done.

shortness-of-life_section-08.originalText: It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on: it will not prolong itself at the command of a king, or at the wish of a nation: as it started on its first day, so it will run: it will never turn aside, never delay. What follows, then? Why! you are busy, but life is hurrying on: death will be here some time or other, and you must attend to him, whether you will or no.
shortness-of-life_section-08.plainEnglish: Time won't make any noise or warn you how fast it's flying by. It moves in silence. No king can command it to slow down. No nation can wish for more of it. Time runs the same way it started on day one. It never turns aside. It never delays. So what happens next? You're busy with your tasks, but life is rushing past. Death will arrive someday, and you'll have to face him whether you want to or not.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom? They live laboriously, in order that they may live better; they fit themselves out for life at the expense of life itself, and cast their thoughts a long way forwards: yet postponement is the greatest waste of life: it wrings day after day from us, and takes away the present by promising something hereafter: there is no such obstacle to true living as waiting, which loses to-day while it is depending on the morrow. You dispose of that which is in the hand of Fortune, and you let go that which is in your own. Whither are you looking, whither are you stretching forward? everything future is uncertain: live now straightway.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Is there anything more crazy than how supposedly wise people think about free time? They work themselves to death so they can live better later. They spend their whole lives preparing to live — using up life itself in the process. They're always thinking far into the future. But putting things off is the biggest waste of life there is. It steals each day from us. It sacrifices the present by promising something better tomorrow. Nothing blocks real living like waiting — losing today while depending on tomorrow. You're betting on what fortune controls, while letting go of what you actually control. Where are you looking? What are you reaching for? Everything in the future is uncertain. Live right now.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: See how the greatest of bards cries to you and sings in wholesome verse as though inspired with celestial fire:— "The best of wretched mortals' days is that Which is the first to fly." Why do you hesitate, says he, why do you stand back? unless you seize it it will have fled: and even if you do seize it, it will still fly. Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: Look at how the greatest poet cries out to you, singing in powerful verse as if inspired by divine fire: 'The best day in our wretched lives is the first one to slip away.' Why do you hesitate? he asks. Why do you hold back? Unless you grab it, it will escape. And even if you do grab it, it will still fly away. We need to use our time as quickly as time itself moves. We should drink from it like we would from a fast-flowing stream that won't flow forever.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: The poet, too, admirably satirizes our boundless thoughts, when he says, not "the first age," but "the first day." Why are you careless and slow while time is flying so fast, and why do you spread out before yourself a vision of long months and years, as many as your greediness requires? he talks with you about one day, and that a fast-fleeting one. There can, then, be no doubt that the best days are those which fly first for wretched, that is, for busy mortals, whose minds are still in their childhood when old age comes upon them, and they reach it unprepared and without arms to combat it.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: A poet makes fun of our endless daydreaming when he says not "the first age" but "the first day." Why are you lazy and slow when time flies so fast? Why do you imagine having long months and years ahead of you — as many as your greed demands? The poet is talking about just one day, and even that day races by. There's no doubt about it: the best days are the first to fly away. This hits wretched people the hardest — busy people whose minds are still childish when old age sneaks up on them. They reach old age completely unprepared, with no weapons to fight it.

shortness-of-life_section-09.originalText: They have never looked forward: they have all of a sudden stumbled upon old age: they never noticed that it was stealing upon them day by day. As conversation, or reading, or deep thought deceives travellers, and they find themselves at their journey's end before they knew that it was drawing near, so in this fast and never-ceasing journey of life, which we make at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake, busy people never notice that they are moving till they are at the end of it.
shortness-of-life_section-09.plainEnglish: They never looked ahead. They stumbled into old age without warning. They never noticed it creeping up on them day by day. Just like travelers get lost in conversation, reading, or deep thought and suddenly arrive at their destination without realizing they were almost there — that's how it is with life's fast, never-ending journey. Whether we're asleep or awake, we move at the same pace. Busy people never notice they're moving until they reach the end.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all. Fabianus, who was none of your lecture-room philosophers, but one of the true antique pattern, used to say, "We ought to fight against the passions by main force, not by skirmishing, and upset their line of battle by a home charge, not by inflicting trifling wounds: I do not approve of dallying with sophisms; they must be crushed, not merely scratched." Yet, in order that sinners may be confronted with their errors, they must be taught, and not merely mourned for.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: If I wanted to break down this argument step by step with proof, I could show you many ways that busy people actually live the shortest lives of all. Fabianus wasn't one of those classroom philosophers — he was the real deal, old school. He used to say, "You have to fight your destructive emotions head-on, not dance around them. Hit them with everything you've got, don't just scratch at them. I don't believe in playing games with clever arguments. Crush these emotions, don't just tickle them." But if we want people to face their mistakes, we need to teach them, not just feel sorry for them.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Life is divided into three parts: that which has been, that which is, and that which is to come: of these three stages, that which we are passing through is brief, that which we are about to pass is uncertain, and that which we have passed is certain: this it is over which Fortune has lost her rights, and which can fall into no other man's power: and this is what busy men lose: for they have no leisure to look back upon the past, and even if they had, they take no pleasure in remembering what they regret: they are, therefore, unwilling to turn their minds to the contemplation of ill-spent time, and they shrink from reviewing a course of action whose faults become glaringly apparent when handled a second time, although they were snatched at when we were under the spell of immediate gratification.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Life has three parts: the past, the present, and the future. The present moment we're living through is brief. The future is uncertain. But the past is set in stone. Fortune can't touch it anymore. No one else can control it. And this is exactly what busy people throw away. They have no time to look back at their past. Even if they did have time, they wouldn't enjoy it — because they'd just remember their mistakes. So they refuse to think about all the time they've wasted. They can't bear to examine their choices, because the second time around, their mistakes become painfully obvious. The first time, those choices seemed appealing because they were caught up in immediate pleasure.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: No one, unless all his acts have been submitted to the infallible censorship of his own conscience, willingly turns his thoughts back upon the past. He who has ambitiously desired, haughtily scorned, passionately vanquished, treacherously deceived, greedily snatched, or prodigally wasted much, must needs fear his own memory; yet this is a holy and consecrated part of our time, beyond the reach of all human accidents, removed from the dominion of Fortune, and which cannot be disquieted by want, fear, or attacks of sickness: this can neither be troubled nor taken away from one: we possess it for ever undisturbed.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: No one likes to look back at their past unless they can honestly say their conscience is clear. Anyone who has chased power, looked down on others, acted out of rage, deceived people, grabbed what they wanted, or thrown away what they had — they're afraid of their own memories. But here's the thing: our past is actually sacred. It's the one part of our time that can't be touched by accident or bad luck. Poverty can't reach it. Fear can't disturb it. Disease can't attack it. Nothing can trouble it or steal it from us. It's ours forever, completely safe.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Our present consists only of single days, and those, too, taken one hour at a time: but all the days of past times appear before us when bidden, and allow themselves to be examined and lingered over, albeit busy men cannot find time for so doing. It is the privilege of a tranquil and peaceful mind to review all the parts of its life: but the minds of busy men are like animals under the yoke, and cannot bend aside or look back. Consequently, their life passes away into vacancy, and as you do no good however much you may pour into a vessel which cannot keep or hold what you put there, so also it matters not how much time you give men if it can find no place to settle in, but leaks away through the chinks and holes of their minds.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: Our present life feels like just one day at a time, even one hour at a time. But all our past days can come back to us when we call them. We can examine them and linger over them — if we're not too busy to do it. Only a calm and peaceful mind can review all the parts of its life. But busy minds are like animals pulling a plow. They can't turn aside or look back. So their life just passes away into nothing. It's like pouring water into a broken jug — no matter how much you pour in, it doesn't matter if the jug can't hold it. The same thing happens when you give time to people whose minds are full of holes. The time just leaks away.

shortness-of-life_section-10.originalText: Present time is very short, so much so that to some it seems to be no time at all; for it is always in motion, and runs swiftly away: it ceases to exist before it comes, and can no more brook delay than can the universe or the host of heaven, whose unresting movement never lets them pause on their way. Busy men, therefore, possess present time, alone, that being so short that they cannot grasp it, and when they are occupied with many things they lose even this.
shortness-of-life_section-10.plainEnglish: The present moment is incredibly short. To some people, it feels like no time at all. It's always moving and rushing past us. It's gone before it even arrives, just like the universe and the stars that never stop moving through space. So busy people only have this present moment — and it's so brief they can't even hold onto it. When they're juggling too many things at once, they lose even this tiny slice of time they have.

shortness-of-life_section-11.originalText: In a word, do you want to know for how short a time they live? see how they desire to live long: broken-down old men beg in their prayers for the addition of a few more years: they pretend to be younger than they are: they delude themselves with their own lies, and are as willing to cheat themselves as if they could cheat Fate at the same time: when at last some weakness reminds them that they are mortal, they die as it were in terror: they may rather be said to be dragged out of this life than to depart from it. They loudly exclaim that they have been fools and have not lived their lives, and declare that if they only survive this sickness they will spend the rest of their lives at leisure: at such times they reflect how uselessly they have laboured to provide themselves with what they have never enjoyed, and how all their toil has gone for nothing:
shortness-of-life_section-11.plainEnglish: Want to know how briefly they really live? Look at how desperately they want to live longer. Old men, falling apart, beg God for just a few more years. They lie about their age. They fool themselves with their own stories, as if they could trick fate itself. When illness finally reminds them they're going to die, they panic. They don't leave this life — they get dragged out of it kicking and screaming. They cry out that they've been fools, that they never really lived. They promise that if they survive this illness, they'll finally start enjoying life. Only then do they see how pointlessly they worked for things they never enjoyed. All that effort was for nothing.

shortness-of-life_section-11.originalText: but those whose life is spent without any engrossing business may well find it ample: no part of it is made over to others, or scattered here and there; no part is entrusted to Fortune, is lost by neglect, is spent in ostentatious giving, or is useless: all of it is, so to speak, invested at good interest. A very small amount of it, therefore, is abundantly sufficient, and so, when his last day arrives, the wise man will not hang back, but will walk with a steady step to meet death.
shortness-of-life_section-11.plainEnglish: But people who don't waste their lives on meaningless busy work will find they have plenty of time. They don't hand pieces of their life over to other people or scatter it in all directions. They don't leave chunks of it up to chance, lose it through carelessness, waste it showing off, or spend it on pointless things. All of their time is invested wisely, like money earning good interest. Even a small amount goes a long way. So when their final day comes, the wise person won't hesitate or pull back. They'll walk forward with steady steps to meet death.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Perhaps you will ask me whom I mean by "busy men"? you need not think that I allude only to those who are hunted out of the courts of justice with dogs at the close of the proceedings, those whom you see either honourably jostled by a crowd of their own clients or contemptuously hustled in visits of ceremony by strangers, who call them away from home to hang about their patron's doors, or who make use of the praetor's sales by auction to acquire infamous gains which some day will prove their own ruin. Some men's leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men's society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men's life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Maybe you're wondering who I mean by "busy men." Don't think I'm only talking about the lawyers who get chased out of court when the day ends, or those you see either proudly surrounded by their own clients or rudely pushed around by strangers during formal visits. I don't just mean those who drag them from home to wait around at their patron's door, or who use the praetor's auctions to make shameful profits that will eventually destroy them. Some people are busy even in their leisure time. In their country house or lying on their couch, completely alone, even though they've withdrawn from all society, they still manage to torment themselves. We shouldn't call such men's lives leisurely — their business is just being lazy.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Would you call a man idle who expends anxious finicking care in the arrangement of his Corinthian bronzes, valuable only through the mania of a few connoisseurs? and who passes the greater part of his days among plates of rusty metal? who sits in the palaestra (shame, that our very vices should be foreign) watching boys wrestling? who distributes his gangs of fettered slaves into pairs according to their age and colour? who keeps athletes of the latest fashion?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Would you call a man lazy who spends hours fussing over his expensive bronze statues — things that are only valuable because a few collectors have gone crazy for them? A man who wastes most of his day staring at old metal plates? Who sits in the gym (how embarrassing that we've even imported our bad habits from abroad) watching boys wrestle? Who sorts his chained slaves into matching pairs by age and skin color? Who keeps trendy athletes like pets?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Why, do you call those men idle, who pass many hours at the barber's while the growth of the past night is being plucked out by the roots, holding councils over each several hair, while the scattered locks are arranged in order and those which fall back are forced forward on to the forehead? How angry they become if the shaver is a little careless, as though he were shearing a _man_! what a white heat they work themselves into if some of their mane is cut away, if some part of it is ill-arranged, if all their ringlets do not lie in regular order! who of them would not rather that the state were overthrown than that his hair should be ruffled? who does not care more for the appearance of his head than for his health? who would not prefer ornament to honour?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you really call these men busy? They spend hours at the barber's shop. They have him pluck out every hair that grew overnight. They hold serious discussions about each individual hair. They carefully arrange their scattered locks and force the ones that fall back onto their foreheads. Watch how angry they get if the barber makes one small mistake — as if he were cutting up a real man! See how furious they become if some of their precious hair gets cut too short, or if one section doesn't look perfect, or if their curls don't lie in perfect rows! Which of them wouldn't rather see the government collapse than have his hairstyle messed up? Who doesn't care more about how his head looks than his actual health? Who wouldn't choose a good appearance over real honor?

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Do you call these men idle, who make a business of the comb and looking-glass? what of those who devote their lives to composing, hearing, and learning songs, who twist their voices, intended by Nature to sound best and simplest when used straightforwardly, through all the turns of futile melodies: whose fingers are always beating time to some music on which they are inwardly meditating; who, when invited to serious and even sad business may be heard humming an air to themselves?—such people are not at leisure, but are busy about trifles.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Do you call these men idle — the ones who spend all their time on their hair and mirrors? What about those who devote their entire lives to writing songs, listening to music, and learning melodies? They twist their voices through pointless musical runs when nature meant them to sound best when used simply. Their fingers are always tapping out some tune they're thinking about. Even when they're called to handle serious or tragic business, you can hear them humming to themselves. These people aren't at leisure — they're busy with nonsense.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: As for their banquets, by Hercules, I cannot reckon them among their unoccupied times when I see with what anxious care they set out their plate, how laboriously they arrange the girdles of their waiters' tunics, how breathlessly they watch to see how the cook dishes up the wild boar, with what speed, when the signal is given, the slave-boys run to perform their duties, how skilfully birds are carved into pieces of the right size, how painstakingly wretched youths wipe up the spittings of drunken men. By these means men seek credit for taste and grandeur, and their vices follow them so far into their privacy that they can neither eat nor drink without a view to effect.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: And their dinner parties? Good God, I can't call those relaxing either. Look at the anxious care they put into arranging the silverware. Watch how they fuss over the servants' uniforms. See how they hold their breath waiting for the cook to present the roast boar just right. Notice how the slave boys sprint to their tasks the moment they're signaled. Watch the skillful carving of birds into perfect portions. See the miserable young servants carefully cleaning up after drunk guests. Through all this, these hosts are trying to impress people with their refined taste and wealth. Their need to show off follows them so deeply into private life that they can't even eat or drink without putting on a performance.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: Nor should I count those men idle who have themselves carried hither and thither in sedans and litters, and who look forward to their regular hour for taking this exercise as though they were not allowed to omit it: men who are reminded by some one else when to bathe, when to swim, when to dine: they actually reach such a pitch of languid effeminacy as not to be able to find out for themselves whether they are hungry.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I wouldn't call those men idle either — the ones who get carried around in chairs and litters, who wait for their scheduled exercise time like it's a sacred ritual they can't skip. These are men who need someone else to tell them when to bathe, when to swim, when to eat. They've become so weakly pampered that they can't even figure out if they're hungry.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: I have heard one of these luxurious folk—if indeed, we ought to give the name of luxury to unlearning the life and habits of a man—when he was carried in men's arms out of the bath and placed in his chair, say inquiringly, "Am I seated?" Do you suppose that such a man as this, who did not know when he was seated, could know whether he was alive, whether he could see, whether he was at leisure? I can hardly say whether I pity him more if he really did not know or if he pretended not to know this.
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: I once heard one of these pampered rich people—though I'm not sure we should call it luxury when someone has forgotten how to be human—ask his servants, "Am I sitting down?" They had just carried him from his bath and put him in his chair. Can you imagine? A man who doesn't know if he's sitting—do you think he knows if he's alive? If he can see? If he has any free time? I honestly can't decide what's worse: if he really didn't know, or if he was just pretending.

shortness-of-life_section-12.originalText: To think that there should be any one who had so far lost his senses through luxury as to take some one else's opinion as to whether he was sitting or not? This man certainly is not at leisure: you must bestow a different title on him: he is sick, or rather dead: he only is at leisure who feels that he is at leisure: but this creature is only half alive, if he wants some one to tell him what position his body is in. How can such a man be able to dispose of any time?
shortness-of-life_section-12.plainEnglish: Can you imagine someone so corrupted by luxury that they need another person to tell them whether they're sitting down or not? This person is definitely not enjoying leisure. You need a different word for him: he's sick, or actually dead. Only someone who knows they're at leisure is truly at leisure. But this poor creature is barely alive if he needs someone else to tell him what position his body is in. How could such a person possibly manage his time?

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: It would take long to describe the various individuals who have wasted their lives over playing at draughts, playing at ball, or toasting their bodies in the sun: men are not at leisure if their pleasures partake of the character of business, for no one will doubt that those persons are laborious triflers who devote themselves to the study of futile literary questions, of whom there is already a great number in Rome also. It used to be a peculiarly Greek disease of the mind to investigate how many rowers Ulysses had, whether the Iliad or the Odyssey was written first, and furthermore, whether they were written by the same author, with other matters of the same stamp, which neither please your inner consciousness if you keep them to yourself, nor make you seem more learned, but only more troublesome, if you publish them abroad.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: I could spend forever listing people who waste their lives playing board games, playing ball, or lying in the sun. These people aren't truly at leisure — their fun has become like work. And no one doubts that scholars who chase pointless questions are just busy fools. We already have plenty of them in Rome too. It used to be a distinctly Greek mental illness — studying how many rowers Odysseus had, whether the Iliad or Odyssey was written first, whether the same person wrote both, and other equally useless questions. Keep these thoughts to yourself and they bring you no joy. Share them and you don't look learned — just annoying.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: See, already this vain longing to learn what is useless has taken hold of the Romans: the other day I heard somebody telling who was the first Roman general who did this or that: Duillius was the first who won a sea-fight, Curius Dentatus was the first who drove elephants in his triumph: moreover, these stories, though they add nothing to real glory, do nevertheless deal with the great deeds of our countrymen: such knowledge is not profitable, yet it claims our attention as a fascinating kind of folly.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Look, this pointless desire to learn useless facts has already infected the Romans. The other day I heard someone explaining who was the first Roman general to do this or that: Duillius was the first to win a naval battle, Curius Dentatus was the first to parade elephants in his victory procession. These stories don't add anything to real glory, but at least they deal with great deeds by our countrymen. This kind of knowledge isn't useful, but it grabs our attention like an entertaining form of foolishness.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: I will even pardon those who want to know who first persuaded the Romans to go on board ship. It was Claudius, who for this reason was surnamed Caudex, because any piece of carpentry formed of many planks was called _caudex_ by the ancient Romans, for which reason public records are called _Codices_, and by old custom the ships which ply on the Tiber with provisions are called _codicariae_. Let us also allow that it is to the point to tell how Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana, and first of the family of the Valerii transferred the name of the captured city to his own, and was called Messana, and how the people gradually corrupted the pronunciation and called him Messalla: or would you let any one find interest in Lucius Sulla having been the first to let lions loose in the circus, they having been previously exhibited in chains, and hurlers of darts having been sent by King Bocchus to kill them?
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: I'll even forgive people who want to know who first convinced the Romans to get on ships. It was Claudius, who got the nickname Caudex because the ancient Romans called anything made from many planks "caudex." That's why public records are called "Codices," and why the old supply boats on the Tiber are called "codicariae." Let's also allow that it might matter to tell how Valerius Corvinus was the first to conquer Messana. He was the first of the Valerius family to take the name of a captured city for himself, calling himself Messana. Over time, people gradually changed how they said it and called him Messalla. Or would you really let someone get interested in how Lucius Sulla was the first to release lions in the circus? Before that, they had only been shown in chains. King Bocchus sent spear-throwers to kill them.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: This may be permitted to their curiosity: but can it serve any useful purpose to know that Pompeius was the first to exhibit eighteen elephants in the circus, who were matched in a mimic battle with some convicts? The leading man in the state, and one who, according to tradition, was noted among the ancient leaders of the state for his transcendent goodness of heart, thought it a notable kind of show to kill men in a manner hitherto unheard of. Do they fight to the death? that is not cruel enough: are they torn to pieces? that is not cruel enough: let them be crushed flat by animals of enormous bulk. It would be much better that such a thing should be forgotten, for fear that hereafter some potentate might hear of it and envy its refined barbarity.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: People love to collect trivia like this: but what's the point of knowing that Pompey was the first to put eighteen elephants in the circus to fight condemned criminals in fake battles? Here was Rome's leading citizen, a man famous among past leaders for his kind heart. And he thought it would be entertaining to kill people in a completely new way. Regular fighting to the death? Not cruel enough. Getting torn apart? Still not cruel enough. Let's have them crushed flat by enormous animals. It would be better if we forgot such things entirely. Otherwise some future ruler might hear about it and want to copy this elegant savagery.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: O, how doth excessive prosperity blind our intellects! at the moment at which he was casting so many troops of wretches to be trampled on by outlandish beasts, when he was proclaiming war between such different creatures, when he was shedding so much blood before the eyes of the Roman people, whose blood he himself was soon to shed even more freely, he thought himself the master of the whole world; yet he afterwards, deceived by the treachery of the Alexandrians, had to offer himself to the dagger of the vilest of slaves, and then at last discovered what an empty boast was his surname of "The Great."
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: How prosperity blinds us! At the very moment Pompey was throwing countless prisoners to foreign beasts, staging battles between exotic animals, and spilling blood before the Roman crowds — blood he would soon spill even more freely — he believed he ruled the world. Yet later, betrayed by the Alexandrians, he had to offer his throat to the blade of the lowest slave. Only then did he learn how empty his title "The Great" really was.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: But to return to the point from which I have digressed, I will prove that even on this very subject some people expend useless pains. The same author tells us that Metellus, when he triumphed after having conquered the Carthaginians in Sicily, was the only Roman who ever had a hundred and twenty captured elephants led before his car: and that Sulla was the last Roman who extended the pomoerium,[7] which it was not the custom of the ancients to extend on account of the conquest of provincial, but only of Italian territory. Is it more useful to know this, than to know that the Mount Aventine, according to him, is outside of the pomoerium, for one of two reasons, either because it was thither that the plebeians seceded, or because when Remus took his auspices on that place the birds which he saw were not propitious: and other stories without number of the like sort, which are either actual falsehoods or much the same as falsehoods?
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: But let me get back to my main point. I want to show you that people waste effort even on this very topic. The same writer tells us that Metellus was the only Roman who ever had 120 captured elephants march in front of his chariot when he celebrated his triumph over the Carthaginians in Sicily. He also says Sulla was the last Roman to extend the pomoerium — the sacred boundary around Rome. The ancients only extended it when they conquered Italian territory, not foreign provinces. Is knowing this really more useful than knowing why Mount Aventine sits outside the pomoerium? According to this writer, it's either because the common people once fled there during a revolt, or because when Remus took his bird omens on that spot, the signs were bad. There are countless other stories just like these — either outright lies or close enough to lies that it doesn't matter.

shortness-of-life_section-13.originalText: for even if you allow that these authors speak in all good faith, if they pledge themselves for the truth of what they write, still, whose mistakes will be made fewer by such stories? whose passions will be restrained? whom will they make more brave, more just, or more gentlemanly? My friend Fabianus used to say that he was not sure that it was not better not to apply oneself to any studies at all than to become interested in these.
shortness-of-life_section-13.plainEnglish: Even if you believe these authors are completely honest and telling the truth, what good does it do? Whose mistakes will their stories prevent? Whose passions will they control? Who will become braver, more just, or more noble from reading them? My friend Fabianus used to say he wasn't sure it wouldn't be better to avoid studying altogether than to get caught up in this stuff.

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them.
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Only philosophers are truly free. They alone really live. They don't just enjoy their own lifetime — they add every century to their own. All the years that came before them become theirs.

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: Unless we are the most ungrateful creatures in the world, we shall regard these noblest of men, the founders of divine schools of thought, as having been born for us, and having prepared life for us: we are led by the labour of others to behold most beautiful things which have been brought out of darkness into light; we are not shut out from any period, we can make our way into every subject, and, if only we can summon up sufficient strength of mind to overstep the narrow limit of human weakness, we have a vast extent of time wherein to disport ourselves: we may argue with Socrates, doubt with Carneades, repose with Epicurus, overcome human nature with the Stoics, out-herod it with the Cynics. Since Nature allows us to commune with every age, why do we not abstract ourselves from our own petty fleeting span of time, and give ourselves up with our whole mind to what is vast, what is eternal, what we share with better men than ourselves?
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Unless we're completely ungrateful, we should see these great thinkers — the founders of the major schools of philosophy — as having been born for our benefit. They prepared a way of life for us. Thanks to their hard work, we can now see beautiful truths that were once hidden in darkness. We're not locked out of any time period. We can enter any subject we want. If we can find the mental strength to break free from our human limitations, we have a vast stretch of time to explore and enjoy. We can debate with Socrates, question everything with Carneades, find peace with Epicurus, rise above human nature with the Stoics, or reject convention entirely with the Cynics. Since nature lets us connect with every age, why do we stay trapped in our own tiny, fleeting moment? Why not give our whole mind to what is vast and eternal — to what we share with men far better than ourselves?

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: Those who gad about in a round of calls, who worry themselves and others, after they have indulged their madness to the full, and crossed every patron's threshold daily, leaving no open door unentered, after they have hawked about their interested greetings in houses of the most various character,—after all, how few people are they able to see out of so vast a city, divided among so many different ruling passions: how many will be moved by sloth, self-indulgence, or rudeness to deny them admittance: how many, after they have long plagued them, will run past them with feigned hurry? how many will avoid coming out through their entrance-hall with its crowds of clients, and will escape by some concealed backdoor? as though it were not ruder to deceive their visitor than to deny him admittance!—how many, half asleep and stupid with yesterday's debauch, can hardly be brought to return the greeting of the wretched man who has broken his own rest in order to wait on that of another, even after his name has been whispered to them for the thousandth time, save by a most offensive yawn of his half-opened lips.
