shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: Think about those people who rush around the city making social calls. They worry themselves sick and drive everyone else crazy too. They chase after their obsession completely. They visit every powerful person's house every single day. They never pass up an open door. They peddle their fake friendly greetings to houses of all different types. But after all this effort, how few people do they actually get to see in such a huge city filled with so many different desires and interests? How many people will be too lazy, too self-indulgent, or just too rude to let them in? How many will torment them for ages, then rush past them pretending to be in a hurry? How many will avoid coming out through their main entrance hall (crowded with clients) and sneak out the back door instead? As if tricking a visitor isn't ruder than just refusing to see them in the first place! And how many are half-asleep and stupid from last night's drinking? Even after their servant whispers the poor visitor's name for the thousandth time, they can barely manage to return his greeting. The best they can do is an insulting yawn through half-open lips. This miserable man broke his own sleep just to attend to theirs.

shortness-of-life_section-14.originalText: We may truly say that those men are pursuing the true path of duty, who wish every day to consort on the most familiar terms with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the rest of those high priests of virtue, with Aristotle and with Theophrastus. None of these men will be "engaged," none of these will fail to send you away after visiting him in a happier frame of mind and on better terms with yourself, none of them will let you leave him empty-handed: yet their society may be enjoyed by all men, and by night as well as by day.
shortness-of-life_section-14.plainEnglish: The people who are truly living right are those who spend time every day with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the other great teachers of virtue — with Aristotle and Theophrastus. None of these men will be "too busy" for you. None will send you away without making you feel happier and more at peace with yourself. None will let you leave empty-handed. And here's the best part: anyone can enjoy their company, day or night.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: None of these men will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to die: none of these will waste your time, but will add his own to it. The talk of these men is not dangerous, their friendship will not lead you to the scaffold, their society will not ruin you in expenses: you may take from them whatsoever you will; they will not prevent your taking the deepest draughts of their wisdom that you please. What blessedness, what a fair old age awaits the man who takes these for his patrons! he will have friends with whom he may discuss all matters, great and small, whose advice he may ask daily about himself, from whom he will hear truth without insult, praise without flattery, and according to whose likeness he may model his own character.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: None of these writers will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to live well. None will waste your time — they'll add their own lifetimes to yours. Their conversations aren't dangerous. Their friendship won't get you executed. Their company won't bankrupt you. You can take whatever you want from them. They won't stop you from drinking deeply from their wisdom. What happiness awaits someone who makes these great minds his guides! He'll have friends to discuss everything with, big and small. He can ask their advice every day. They'll tell him the truth without being cruel. They'll praise him without flattery. And he can shape his own character based on their example.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: We are wont to say that we are not able to choose who our parents should be, but that they were assigned to us by chance; yet we may be born just as we please: there are several families of the noblest intellects: choose which you would like to belong to: by your adoption you will not receive their name only, but also their property, which is not intended to be guarded in a mean and miserly spirit: the more persons you divide it among the larger it becomes. These will open to you the path which leads to eternity, and will raise you to a height from whence none shall cast you down.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: We usually say we can't choose our parents — that we're stuck with whoever chance gave us. But we can choose to be born into any intellectual family we want. There are many noble minds to pick from. Choose which one you'd like to belong to. When you adopt their ideas, you don't just get their name. You also get their wealth of wisdom. And this wealth isn't meant to be hoarded like a miser guards his coins. The more people you share it with, the richer it becomes. These great thinkers will show you the path to immortality. They'll lift you to heights where no one can knock you down.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: By this means alone can you prolong your mortal life, nay, even turn it into an immortal one. High office, monuments, all that ambition records in decrees or piles up in stone, soon passes away: lapse of time casts down and ruins everything; but those things on which Philosophy has set its seal are beyond the reach of injury: no age will discard them or lessen their force, each succeeding century will add somewhat to the respect in which they are held: for we look upon what is near us with jealous eyes, but we admire what is further off with less prejudice.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: This is the only way to extend your mortal life — or even make it immortal. High office, monuments, everything that ambition records in decrees or builds in stone — it all fades away quickly. Time destroys everything. But the things that Philosophy has marked as its own cannot be harmed. No age will throw them out or weaken them. Each new century will respect them even more. We look at what's close to us with jealous, critical eyes. But we admire what's distant with less bias.

shortness-of-life_section-15.originalText: The wise man's life, therefore, includes much: he is not hedged in by the same limits which confine others: he alone is exempt from the laws by which mankind is governed: all ages serve him like a god. If any time be past, he recals it by his memory; if it be present, he uses it; if it be future, he anticipates it: his life is a long one because he concentrates all times into it.
shortness-of-life_section-15.plainEnglish: The wise person's life contains much more than most. They aren't trapped by the same limits that confine everyone else. They alone are free from the laws that govern ordinary people. All of history serves them like a god. If time has passed, they bring it back through memory. If time is present, they use it fully. If time is future, they prepare for it. Their life is long because they gather all times into it.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future: when they reach the end of it the poor wretches learn too late that they were busied all the while that they were doing nothing. You need not think, because sometimes they call for death, that their lives are long: their folly torments them with vague passions which lead them into the very things of which they are afraid: they often, therefore, wish for death because they live in fear.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: The people with the shortest and most miserable lives are those who forget their past, ignore their present, and fear their future. When they reach the end, these poor souls realize too late that they stayed busy their whole lives while accomplishing nothing. Don't think their lives are long just because they sometimes wish for death. Their foolishness torments them with confused desires that drive them toward the very things they fear. So they often wish for death precisely because they live in fear.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Neither is it, as you might think, a proof of the length of their lives that they often find the days long, that they often complain how slowly the hours pass until the appointed time arrives for dinner: for whenever they are left without their usual business, they fret helplessly in their idleness, and know not how to arrange or to spin it out. They betake themselves, therefore, to some business, and all the intervening time is irksome to them; they would wish, by Hercules, to skip over it, just as they wish to skip over the intervening days before a gladiatorial contest or some other time appointed for a public spectacle or private indulgence: all postponement of what they wish for is grievous to them.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: Don't think that people complaining about long, boring days proves they actually have plenty of time. When they whine about how slowly the hours crawl by until dinner, or how the day drags on — that's not a sign of abundance. It's the opposite. When these people have nothing to occupy them, they become restless and anxious. They don't know what to do with themselves. So they frantically look for some activity to fill the void. Any gap in their schedule feels unbearable. They want to fast-forward through it, just like they want to skip ahead to the gladiator fights or whatever show or pleasure they're looking forward to. Any delay in getting what they want feels like torture.

shortness-of-life_section-16.originalText: Yet the very time which they enjoy is brief and soon past, and is made much briefer by their own fault: for they run from one pleasure to another, and are not able to devote themselves consistently to one passion: their days are not long, but odious to them: on the other hand, how short they find the nights which they spend with courtezans or over wine? Hence arises that folly of the poets who encourage the errors of mankind by their myths, and declare that Jupiter to gratify his voluptuous desires doubled the length of the night. Is it not adding fuel to our vices to name the gods as their authors, and to offer our distempers free scope by giving them deity for an example? How can the nights for which men pay so dear fail to appear of the shortest? they lose the day in looking forward to the night, and lose the night through fear of the dawn.
shortness-of-life_section-16.plainEnglish: Even the time they do enjoy is brief and fleeting. And they make it even shorter through their own mistakes. They jump from one pleasure to another, unable to stick with any single passion. Their days don't feel long — they feel tedious. But how short the nights seem when they're with prostitutes or drinking! This is where poets get their foolish ideas. They encourage human weakness with their stories. They claim Jupiter doubled the length of a night to satisfy his sexual desires. Isn't this just adding fuel to our vices? They make the gods responsible for our bad behavior. They give us divine permission to be sick. How can nights that cost so much money not feel incredibly short? People waste their days looking forward to night, then waste their nights dreading the morning.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Such men's very pleasures are restless and disturbed by various alarms, and at the most joyous moment of all there rises the anxious thought: "How long will this last?" This frame of mind has led kings to weep over their power, and they have not been so much delighted at the grandeur of their position, as they have been terrified by the end to which it must some day come. That most arrogant Persian king, when his army stretched over vast plains and could not be counted but only measured, burst into tears at the thought that in less than a hundred years none of all those warriors would be alive; yet their death was brought upon them by the very man who wept over it, who was about to destroy some of them by sea, some on land, some in battle, and some in flight, and who would in a very short space of time put an end to those about whose hundredth year he showed such solicitude.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Even their pleasures are restless and full of worry. Right in the middle of their happiest moments, an anxious thought creeps in: "How long will this last?" This mindset has made kings cry over their own power. They're not so much thrilled by their greatness as they are terrified by how it will eventually end. Take that arrogant Persian king. His army spread across vast plains — so many soldiers you couldn't count them, only measure the space they covered. He burst into tears thinking that in less than a hundred years, none of those warriors would still be alive. But here's the irony: their deaths would come from the very man weeping over them. He was about to destroy some by sea, some on land, some in battle, some while they fled. In just a short time, he would kill the very men whose hundred-year lifespans he was so worried about.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Why need we wonder at their very joys being mixed with fear? they do not rest upon any solid grounds, but are disturbed by the same emptiness from which they spring. What must we suppose to be the misery of such times as even they acknowledge to be wretched, when even the joys by which they elevate themselves and raise themselves above their fellows are of a mixed character. All the greatest blessings are enjoyed with fear, and no thing is so untrustworthy as extreme prosperity: we require fresh strokes of good fortune to enable us to keep that which we are enjoying, and even those of our prayers which are answered require fresh prayers. Everything for which we are dependent on chance is uncertain: the higher it rises, the more opportunities it has of falling. Moreover, no one takes any pleasure in what is about to fall into ruin: very wretched, therefore, as well as very short must be the lives of those who work very hard to gain what they must work even harder to keep: they obtain what they wish with infinite labour, and they hold what they have obtained with fear and trembling.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Why should we be surprised that even their joys are mixed with fear? Their happiness has no solid foundation. It's shaken by the same emptiness that created it. Imagine how miserable their worst times must be, when even the joys that make them feel superior to others are tainted with worry. All our greatest blessings come with fear. Nothing is less reliable than extreme success. We need fresh streaks of good luck just to hold onto what we already have. Even our answered prayers need more prayers to keep them safe. Anything that depends on chance is uncertain. The higher it climbs, the more ways it can fall. Besides, no one enjoys something that's about to collapse. So the lives of people who work incredibly hard to get things — and then work even harder to keep them — must be both miserable and short. They get what they want through endless struggle. Then they hold onto it with fear and trembling.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Meanwhile they take no account of time, of which they will never have a fresh and larger supply: they substitute new occupations for old ones, one hope leads to another, one ambition to another: they do not seek for an end to their wretchedness, but they change its subject. Do our own preferments trouble us? nay, those of other men occupy more of our time. Have we ceased from our labours in canvassing? then we begin others in voting. Have we got rid of the trouble of accusation? then we begin that of judging. Has a man ceased to be a judge? then he becomes an examiner. Has he grown old in the salaried management of other people's property? then he becomes occupied with his own.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Meanwhile, they pay no attention to time — something they can never get more of. They replace old activities with new ones. One hope leads to another hope, one ambition to another ambition. They don't try to end their misery. They just change what makes them miserable. Are we worried about our own promotions? No, we spend even more time obsessing over other people's careers. Have we stopped campaigning for office? Then we start campaigning for someone else. Are we done with prosecuting cases? Then we start judging them. Has someone stopped being a judge? Then he becomes an investigator. Has he grown old managing other people's money for pay? Then he gets busy managing his own.

shortness-of-life_section-17.originalText: Marius is discharged from military service; he becomes consul many times: Quintius is eager to reach the end of his dictatorship; he will be called a second time from the plough: Scipio marched against the Carthaginians before he was of years sufficient for so great an undertaking; after he has conquered Hannibal, conquered Antiochus, been the glory of his own consulship and the surety for that of his brother, he might, had he wished it, have been set on the same pedestal with Jupiter; but civil factions will vex the saviour of the state, and he who when a young man disdained to receive divine honours, will take pride as an old man in obstinately remaining in exile. We shall never lack causes of anxiety, either pleasurable or painful: our life will be pushed along from one business to another: leisure will always be wished for, and never enjoyed.
shortness-of-life_section-17.plainEnglish: Marius leaves the army and becomes consul many times. Quintius can't wait to finish his term as dictator — then they'll call him back from his farm for a second round. Scipio marched against Carthage when he was still too young for such a huge job. After he defeated Hannibal and Antiochus, brought glory to his own consulship and secured his brother's, he could have been worshipped like a god if he wanted. But political enemies will torment the man who saved the state. The same person who rejected divine honors as a young man will stubbornly pride himself on staying in exile as an old man. We'll never run out of things to worry about — whether they bring us joy or pain. Life will push us from one task to the next. We'll always want leisure time, but we'll never actually enjoy it.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: Whefore, my dearest Paulinus, tear yourself away from the common herd, and since you have seen more rough weather than one would think from your age, betake yourself at length to a more peaceful haven: reflect what waves you have sailed through, what storms you have endured in private life, and brought upon yourself in public. Your courage has been sufficiently displayed by many toilsome and wearisome proofs; try how it will deal with leisure: the greater, certainly the better part of your life, has been given to your country; take now some part of your time for yourself as well. I do not urge you to practise a dull or lazy sloth, or to drown all your fiery spirit in the pleasures which are dear to the herd: that is not rest: you can find greater works than all those which you have hitherto so manfully carried out, upon which you may employ yourself in retirement and security.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: So, my dear Paulinus, pull yourself away from the crowd. You've weathered more storms than someone your age should have to face. It's time to find a calmer harbor. Think about all the waves you've sailed through. Think about the storms you've endured in your private life, and the ones you brought on yourself in public service. You've proven your courage many times over through exhausting trials. Now try how it handles peace and quiet. The greater part of your life — certainly the better part — has been given to your country. Take some time for yourself now. I'm not telling you to become lazy or dull. Don't drown your fire in the cheap pleasures that satisfy the masses. That's not real rest. You can find greater work than anything you've done so far — work you can do in retirement and safety.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: You manage the revenues of the entire world, as unselfishly as though they belonged to another, as laboriously as if they were your own, as scrupulously as though they belonged to the public: you win love in an office in which it is hard to avoid incurring hatred; yet, believe me, it is better to understand your own mind than to understand the corn-market. Take away that keen intellect of yours, so well capable of grappling with the greatest subjects, from a post which may be dignified, but which is hardly fitted to render life happy, and reflect that you did not study from childhood all the branches of a liberal education merely in order that many thousand tons of corn might safely be entrusted to your charge: you have given us promise of something greater and nobler than this.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: You manage the world's finances as unselfishly as if the money belonged to someone else, as carefully as if it were your own, and as honestly as if it were public funds. You've won people's love in a job where most people end up being hated. But believe me — it's better to understand your own mind than to understand the grain market. Take that sharp mind of yours, which can handle the biggest problems, away from a job that might be respectable but won't make you happy. Remember: you didn't study all those subjects as a child just so you could be trusted with thousands of tons of grain. You promised us something greater and better than this.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: There will never be any want of strict economists or of laborious workers: slow-going beasts of burden are better suited for carrying loads than well-bred horses, whose generous swiftness no one would encumber with a heavy pack. Think, moreover, how full of risk is the great task which you have undertaken: you have to deal with the human stomach: a hungry people will not endure reason, will not be appeased by justice, and will not hearken to any prayers.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: There will always be plenty of penny-pinchers and hard workers. Slow pack animals are better for heavy loads than fine horses — no one would weigh down a thoroughbred's natural speed with a heavy burden. Think about how dangerous the job you've taken on really is. You're dealing with people's stomachs. Hungry people won't listen to reason, won't be satisfied by justice, and won't pay attention to any pleas.

shortness-of-life_section-18.originalText: Only just a few days ago, when G. Caesar perished, grieving for nothing so much (if those in the other world can feel grief) as that the Roman people did not die with him, there was said to be only enough corn for seven or eight days' consumption: while he was making bridges with ships[9] and playing with the resources of the empire, want of provisions, the worst evil that can befall even a besieged city, was at hand: his imitation of a crazy outlandish and misproud king very nearly ended in ruin, famine, and the general revolution which follows famine. What must then have been the feelings of those who had the charge of supplying the city with corn, who were in danger of stoning, of fire and sword, of Gaius himself? With consummate art they concealed the vast internal evil by which the state was menaced, and were quite right in so doing; for some diseases must be cured without the patient's knowledge: many have died through discovering what was the matter with them.
shortness-of-life_section-18.plainEnglish: Just a few days ago, when Caligula died, he was probably grieving for nothing more than this (if the dead can grieve): the Roman people hadn't died with him. At the time of his death, Rome only had enough grain stored up for seven or eight days. While he was busy building bridges out of ships and playing around with the empire's resources, the city was facing starvation — the worst disaster that can hit even a city under siege. His imitation of some crazy foreign tyrant nearly brought total ruin, famine, and the chaos that always follows famine. Imagine how the officials in charge of the grain supply must have felt. They faced being stoned to death, burned alive, or killed by the sword — maybe even by Caligulus himself. They used great skill to hide this massive threat to the state, and they were absolutely right to do so. Some diseases have to be cured without the patient knowing about them. Many people have died simply from finding out what was wrong with them.

shortness-of-life_section-19.originalText: Betake yourself to these quieter, safer, larger fields of action: do you think that there can be any comparison between seeing that corn is deposited in the public granary without being stolen by the fraud or spoilt by the carelessness of the importer, that it does not suffer from damp or overheating, and that it measures and weighs as much as it ought, and beginning the study of sacred and divine knowledge, which will teach you of what elements the gods are formed, what are their pleasures, their position, their form? to what changes your soul has to look forward? where Nature will place us when we are dismissed from our bodies? what that principle is which holds all the heaviest particles of our universe in the middle, suspends the lighter ones above, puts fire highest of all, and causes the stars to rise in their courses, with many other matters, full of marvels? Will you not cease to grovel on earth and turn your mind's eye on these themes? nay, while your blood still flows swiftly, before your knees grow feeble, you ought to take the better path.
shortness-of-life_section-19.plainEnglish: Turn to these quieter, safer, larger fields of action. Do you think there's any comparison between checking that grain gets stored in public warehouses without being stolen or ruined by careless importers — making sure it doesn't get damp or overheated, and that it weighs what it should — and beginning to study sacred, divine knowledge? This knowledge will teach you what the gods are made of, what gives them pleasure, where they live, what they look like. It will show you what changes await your soul, where Nature will place us when we leave our bodies, what force keeps the heaviest parts of our universe in the center while suspending lighter things above, puts fire at the top, and makes the stars move in their paths — along with countless other marvels. Won't you stop crawling around on earth and turn your mind's eye to these great questions? Do it now, while your blood still flows strong, before your knees grow weak. You should take the better path.

shortness-of-life_section-19.originalText: In this course of life there await you many good things, such as love and practice of the virtues, forgetfulness of passions, knowledge of how to live and die, deep repose. The position of all busy men is unhappy, but most unhappy of all is that of those who do not even labour at their own affairs, but have to regulate their rest by another man's sleep, their walk by another man's pace, and whose very love and hate, the freest things in the world, are at another's bidding. If such men wish to know how short their lives are, let them think how small a fraction of them is their own.
shortness-of-life_section-19.plainEnglish: Life offers you many good things: learning to love and practice virtue, letting go of destructive emotions, knowing how to live well and die peacefully, and finding deep rest. All busy people are unhappy. But the most miserable are those who don't even work on their own projects. They have to sleep when someone else says to sleep. They walk at someone else's pace. Even their love and hate — the most personal things we have — happen on someone else's command. If these people want to know how short their lives really are, they should think about how little of their time actually belongs to them.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life. Men throw away all their years in order to have one year named after them as consul: some lose their lives during the early part of the struggle, and never reach the height to which they aspired: some after having submitted to a thousand indignities in order to reach the crowning dignity, have the miserable reflexion that the only result of their labours will be the inscription on their tombstone.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: So when you see someone wearing fancy robes of office, when you hear their name praised all over the forum — don't be jealous. They paid for those honors by throwing away years of their life. People waste their entire lives just to have one year named after them as consul. Some die in the early stages of climbing the ladder, never reaching the heights they dreamed of. Others endure a thousand humiliations to reach the top, only to realize with horror that all their work will amount to nothing more than words carved on their tombstone.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: Some, while telling off extreme old age, like youth, for new aspirations, have found it fail from sheer weakness amid great and presumptuous enterprises. It is a shameful ending, when a man's breath deserts him in a court of justice, while, although well stricken in years, he is still striving to gain the sympathies of an ignorant audience for some obscure litigant: it is base to perish in the midst of one's business, wearied with living sooner than with working; shameful, too, to die in the act of receiving payments, amid the laughter of one's long-expectant heir.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: Some people, even in extreme old age, chase new ambitions like young people do. But their bodies fail them in the middle of these grand, overreaching projects. It's embarrassing when someone's breath gives out in a courtroom while they're still trying to win over an ignorant crowd for some unknown client — even though they're ancient. It's pathetic to collapse at your desk, worn out by life before you're worn out by work. And it's shameful to die while collecting payments, with your heir standing there laughing because they've been waiting so long.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: I cannot pass over an an instance which occurs to me: Turannius was an old man of the most painstaking exactitude, who after entering upon his ninetieth year, when he had by G. Caesar's own act been relieved of his duties as collector of the revenue, ordered himself to be laid out on his bed and mourned for as though he were dead. The whole house mourned for the leisure of its old master, and did not lay aside its mourning until his work was restored to him. Can men find such pleasure in dying in harness? Yet many are of the same mind: they retain their wish for labour longer than their capacity for it, and fight against their bodily weakness; they think old age an evil for no other reason than because it lays them on the shelf.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: I have to share a story that comes to mind: Turannius was an incredibly meticulous old man. When he turned ninety, Emperor Gaius Caesar personally relieved him of his job as tax collector. What did Turannius do? He had himself laid out on his bed like a corpse and mourned as if he were dead. His entire household mourned their old master's retirement and refused to stop mourning until he got his job back. Can you believe it? Some people actually find pleasure in working themselves to death. And many others think the same way. They want to keep working long after their bodies can handle it. They fight their own weakness. They think old age is terrible for one reason only — because it forces them to retire.

shortness-of-life_section-20.originalText: The law does not enrol a soldier after his fiftieth year, or require a senator's attendance after his sixtieth: but men have more difficulty in obtaining their own consent than that of the law to a life of leisure. Meanwhile, while they are plundering and being plundered, while one is disturbing another's repose, and all are being made wretched alike, life remains without profit, without pleasure, without any intellectual progress: no one keeps death well before his eyes, no one refrains from far-reaching hopes. Some even arrange things which lie beyond their own lives, such as huge sepulchral buildings, the dedication of public works, and exhibitions to be given at their funeral-pyre, and ostentatious processions: but, by Hercules, the funerals of such men ought to be conducted by the light of torches and wax tapers, as though they had lived but a few days.
shortness-of-life_section-20.plainEnglish: The law won't enlist a soldier after fifty or require a senator to show up after sixty. But people have a much harder time giving themselves permission to retire than getting it from the law. Meanwhile, while they're all stealing from each other and ruining each other's peace, making everyone miserable, life passes by with no profit, no pleasure, no learning. No one keeps death in mind. No one stops making grand plans for the distant future. Some even plan things that will happen after they're dead — massive tombs, public monuments, elaborate funeral games, showy processions. But honestly, these people's funerals should be lit with torches and candles like they were infants who lived only a few days.
